generalizedRange: Rivers of northern India and Nepal
hook: A crocodile with a hundred teeth — and no taste for anything but fish.

story.text: The gharial's snout seems impossible: a yard of slender jaw set with about a hundred needle teeth, too thin to threaten anything but fish.
It hunts near the river bottom with swift sideways snaps, and on land it can only slide on its belly between water and warm sand.
Mature males grow a hollow knob at the snout's tip — the ghara, named for an Indian clay pot — that turns their calls into buzzing whistles.
Since the 1940s the species declined by about 98 percent; by the mid-1970s, fifty or sixty survived in India.
The rivers themselves are being unmade: sand mining strips the nesting banks, dams starve the deep pools, and fishing nets drown the long-jawed swimmers.
A female lays about forty eggs in a sandbank and guards the nest alone.
Recovery is under way one release at a time: nearly a thousand captive-reared young gharials have entered the Ganga's rivers since 2009.
Wild adults have climbed from about two hundred to about six hundred and fifty in little more than a decade.
In Nepal, community Gharial Guard Groups patrol the rivers of Chitwan, keeping watch over the nests.
To witness the gharial is to take the side of wild rivers — deep pools, clean sandbanks, room to bask.

editorial.notes: Card v2 drafted from verified Smithsonian, SDZWA, WWF-India, ZSL, and Madras Crocodile Bank pages. Lifespan omitted — no authoritative figure exists (SDZWA: 'not reported'). The popular 'males guard creches of hundreds of hatchlings' claim was unverifiable and contradicts Smithsonian's sole-female-care statement — excluded. Population ~650 wild adults is WWF-India's 2019 figure.

reproduction.text: About forty eggs in a sandbank nest, hatching after roughly seventy days. The mother guards nest and hatchlings alone — her jaws, unlike other crocodilians', are too narrow to carry her young.

insight.text: The male's ghara covers his nostrils and works as a resonator: gharials buzz and whistle where other crocodiles hiss.
